medical.programmeSourceScope: The item packet’s 2024-era directory label “Medical Oncology Fellowships” points to Dana-Farber. The current official page presents the adult clinical physician training as a joint Dana-Farber/MGB Hematology/Oncology fellowship with named Hematology/Oncology and Classical Hematology tracks, plus a separately linked pediatric programme. The course follows only adult medical-oncology content in the ABIM blueprint; separate tracks are named rather than collapsed. The page is institutional programme information, not an ACGME accreditation lookup or complete didactic schedule. Research years are not converted to clinical teaching hours.
sourceCaveats: No saved task-specific MED-117 research artifacts were present in the named prior job folder; current search and fetch research was conducted.

The official programme website calls the adult offering Hematology/Oncology and identifies Classical Hematology separately; “Medical Oncology Fellowships” in the packet is a directory label, not the full current programme title.
ABIM Medical Oncology and Hematology are separate subspecialty certifications; completing a local course does not confer eligibility. Pediatric Hematology-Oncology uses a separate ABP route.
ACGME public program requirements and ABIM blueprint are not the same thing as a local rotation list, official fellowship lecture schedule, or exam bank.

Public Sylvester-linked 2017 YouTube recordings were found, but public duration metadata probing was blocked by YouTube player-response/bot checks. No video was counted; direct free playability is unverified. This is not a claim the videos are unavailable.
Clinical content is date-sensitive. Review NCI PDQ and relevant primary guidance at the time of use. No clinician has reviewed this course. No patient data/image is copied.

topicGaps: The publicly observed, unique ready-recording ledger totals 17.9353 hours; the 36-hour floor still has a residual of 18.0647 hours. Authored scripts and target minutes are not rendered media and contribute zero.

Current accessible recordings are unevenly distributed: disease-specific material is concentrated in thoracic cancer, pancreatic tumor biology, ovarian hereditary risk, germ-cell biology, bladder mechanisms, glioblastoma and head/neck care-access research. Several are mechanistic or research talks, not clinical decision lessons.

No suitable verified current full-length recordings were located for comprehensive breast treatment, prostate and renal-cell clinical pathways, hematologic disease-group breadth, cervical/endometrial/uterine sarcoma, colorectal/hepatobiliary/upper-GI/NET disease management, melanoma, sarcoma, unknown primary, thyroid/salivary/nasopharyngeal cancers, or broad evidence-appraisal/trial-ethics instruction.

Treatment complications are only sampled (tumor lysis and cardio-oncology); the recording set does not supply comprehensive current toxicity triage, dose/contraindication teaching, or clinical protocols.

Palliative and survivorship coverage is inadequate: one emerging psychedelic/regulatory research talk is not a general symptom/pain-management curriculum. Communication, end-of-life, fertility, late effects, cost/access and equity need additional current source-led episodes and qualified review.

Older 2014 breast metastasis biology and any experimental/mechanistic recording require explicit separation from dated efficacy/indication claims. The unknown-duration Sylvester 2017 videos remain uncounted.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A board-style stem gives tumor response percentages from an uncontrolled single-arm trial and asks whether the new regimen improves survival over standard care. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: The regimen improves overall survival because response is higher.
The results establish comparative survival benefit.
The response signal is hypothesis-generating; comparative survival benefit is not established without an appropriate comparison and outcome data.
The study is invalid because all single-arm trials are unethical.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Response is not interchangeable with overall survival, and an uncontrolled design cannot by itself establish comparative benefit. Interpret design, endpoint, uncertainty and clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult patient asks whether ABIM Medical Oncology certification is automatically conferred on completion of a fellowship carrying a Hematology/Oncology title. Best answer?

options.text: Yes, the programme title itself confers both certificates.
No. ABIM has separate certification requirements and examinations; training, competence/licensure requirements and board policies must be met.
Yes, if the fellowship includes research.
No, because ABIM has no medical oncology examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM publishes a Medical Oncology Certification Examination and separate policies. A title or self-study course does not establish eligibility or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hypothetical lung tumor is reported as adenocarcinoma. Before selecting a systemic treatment pathway in a case discussion, which next step is most responsible?

options.text: Assume all adenocarcinomas share one driver and choose therapy.
Review stage, histology, relevant biomarker/molecular testing, clinical context and current authoritative evidence; identify missing information.
Use a 2017 lecture as the only current source.
Skip pathology review if imaging suggests lung primary.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABIM blueprint emphasizes diagnosis/testing and treatment decisions; an evidence-based plan requires context and appropriate diagnostic information. A dated lecture is not a current standard.

practiceQuestions.stem: A randomized study reports a hazard ratio of 0.80 for an endpoint. Which interpretation is safest without additional information?

options.text: There is a 20-percentage-point absolute risk reduction.
The instantaneous event hazard estimate is 20% lower in the intervention arm under the model; assess confidence interval, endpoint, follow-up, assumptions and absolute effects.
Every patient lives 20% longer.
The intervention is proven superior regardless of statistical uncertainty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A hazard ratio is not an absolute risk difference or individual survival extension. Confidence interval, proportional hazards, follow-up, baseline risk and patient-centered outcomes matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is considering using an image from a de-identified TCIA lung imaging collection in a public slide deck. What is the best practice?

options.text: De-identification means every image is public domain.
Check the exact collection’s access and data-use license, follow its terms, and avoid copying/rehosting unless explicitly permitted.
Remove the source attribution and share it.
Patient images can be reused freely if the patient name is hidden.

practiceQuestions.rationale: De-identification and public access do not equal an unrestricted reuse license. Collection-level licenses and conditions govern downstream use.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow has one programme year described as intensive clinical training followed by two or more years of research. Which inference is justified from the public programme description?

options.text: This proves every graduate is eligible for every ABIM subspecialty exam.
This describes the programme’s public training structure, but individual board eligibility and required training/competence must be checked against current board rules and the trainee record.
Research years automatically count as clinical months.
The programme is not physician training.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Programme structure and board eligibility are different claims. ABIM specifies training and competence criteria; the public page does not guarantee an individual’s eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional case, a patient with advanced cancer says symptom relief and time at home matter more than additional disease-directed treatment. Which communication response best fits oncology practice?

options.text: Assume palliative care means stopping all cancer care.
Elicit the patient’s goals, explain options and uncertainties, discuss supportive/palliative care alongside other appropriate care, and coordinate a shared plan.
Avoid discussing prognosis.
Promise that a treatment will meet the goal.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint explicitly includes palliative care, survivorship and communication; a goals-aligned conversation should be honest, individualized and non-coercive.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner’s self-test score is high on eight original course questions. What can be concluded?

options.text: The learner is board-ready and guaranteed to pass.
The learner has demonstrated competence in unsupervised oncology practice.
The result is a limited formative signal only; these questions are neither validated nor official and do not establish board readiness or clinical competence.
The score guarantees eligibility for ABIM certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These original questions are educational, unvalidated and not official exam items. Board eligibility and clinical competence require processes defined by the relevant institutions and boards.

title: Radiation Oncology Residency
prerequisites: This is advanced independent study for learners with prior medical-school-level anatomy, physiology, pathology, oncology and statistics; it is not a substitute for MD/DO education or a residency.
Basic algebra, graph reading, SI units and introductory physics/biology are required; complete Unit 1 foundations as review.
No equipment, patient, procedure, source-handling or clinical practice is authorized by course access.
objectives: Interpret the published ABR radiation oncology certification outline and distinguish accreditation, institutional curriculum and board certification.
Explain core radiation physics, radiobiology, common modalities, planning concepts, safety and limits of simple models.
Structure source-grounded clinical case discussions spanning ABR-published adult, pediatric and benign disease domains.
Appraise uncertainty, evidence, patient goals, professional boundaries, privacy, ethics and team-based care.
Use public case/contouring repositories lawfully by linking and checking terms rather than copying protected content.

units.title: Radiation and cancer biology; quantitative foundations
objectives: Explain direct/indirect DNA damage, repair, cell-cycle response, oxygen effect, LET/RBE, fractionation and normal-tissue effects at a conceptual level.
Use the linear-quadratic BED expression in a clearly hypothetical educational calculation and state its model limitations.
Distinguish physical quantities, absorbed dose, radiobiologic effect and clinical prescription; recognize when a medical physicist is essential.
topics: DNA damage and repair; cell survival; 4/5 Rs; OER and RBE; tumour microenvironment; normal tissue response; α/β and BED; clinical interpretation limits
boardDomains: Radiation and Cancer Biology Qualifying Exam: all 10 domains
Medical Physics Qualifying Exam: fundamental basis
units.casePractice: Use abstract dose/fractionation examples only; do not infer a treatment prescription.
units.assessment: Closed-book concept map plus two model-limited calculations; rubric: mechanisms 40%, quantitative setup 30%, caveats 30%.

units.title: Clinical workflow, diagnosis, staging and multimodality decision framing
objectives: Sequence a defensible educational case discussion from tissue diagnosis and staging evidence to goals, modality options, simulation and follow-up.
Describe external beam, brachytherapy and systemic radionuclide therapy without conflating their delivery or scope.
State what patient/context information is missing before a case can be interpreted; incorporate performance, comorbidity, goals and team input.
topics: Pathology and staging; multidisciplinary care; intent; external beam vs internal brachytherapy vs systemic radiation; consultation; follow-up; patient communication
boardDomains: Clinical Radiation Oncology: diagnosis/staging, modalities, sequencing, benign disease, palliation
units.casePractice: Fictional vignette and a source-based evidence map; no individual treatment recommendation.
units.assessment: One-page case framing with explicit missing-data list and competing options; rubric: diagnosis/stage provenance 25%, integration 25%, goals/uncertainty 25%, communication 25%.

units.title: CNS and spine: primary tumours, metastases and neurologic emergencies
objectives: Organize CNS case interpretation around histology, anatomy, imaging and treatment goal.

Recognize symptoms potentially consistent with an oncologic emergency and escalate for urgent clinician assessment rather than making an online treatment decision.
topics: Gliomas; brain metastases; SRS; whole brain; CNS lymphoma; spine; cord compression; pediatric CNS/CSI
boardDomains: Clinical Radiation Oncology: CNS; pediatric; emergencies; anatomy; field design; toxicity
units.casePractice: ARROCase-linked CNS/spine learning; view at source only and obey source-specific case terms.
units.assessment: Structured oral presentation: diagnostic evidence, anatomy, options, urgent red flags, uncertainty.

units.title: Head and neck: anatomy, nodal pathways and multimodality care

boardDomains: Clinical Radiation Oncology: head and neck; pathology; staging; volumes; toxicity
units.casePractice: Inspect one source-hosted contouring example; annotate only learning points in text, no screenshots redistributed.
units.assessment: Anatomic sketch and short multimodality memo; rubric: anatomy 40%, source traceability 30%, limits/safety 30%.

units.title: Thoracic oncology: lung and mediastinum

assignment.deliverable: One-page distinction among official Hopkins programme, ACGME accreditation requirements, ABR certification pathway, and this independent course.

assignment.title: Multidisciplinary fictional case memo

assessment.formative: 10 original single-best-answer questions with cited explanations; unit checks and source-based case discussions.

assessment.passClaim: No passing score guarantees ABR success, competency, training credit, licensure or clinical action.

studyHours.basis: A transparent self-study plan, not training credit: 83.4347 hours of unique observed public recordings; 31 hours of selected ABR/NCI/ACGME reading; 25 hours of unit notes/case reasoning; 12 hours assignments; 8.5653 hours formative/oral review. Workload is a planning allocation only and does not represent residency equivalence or clinical practice.

topicGaps: No public complete Hopkins lecture schedule or comprehensive institution-owned lecture series was found; its page describes recurring didactics but does not expose a full curriculum or itemized hours.

Recorded lecture coverage is strong for core adult CNS, head/neck, thoracic, breast, GI, GU, gynecologic and hematologic/pediatric topics. Depth and currency vary by video; board study guides are dated (clinical outline labeled 2025, physics guide 2023, biology guide 2022).

Selected topics needing focused source review/optional new teaching include detailed brachytherapy workflow, systemic radionuclide safety, particle therapy uncertainties, image guidance/QA, trial-applicability critique, rare/benign disease, pediatric late effects and site-specific contemporary guidance. Planned clips below are not ready videos and add zero counted hours.

boardNames: American Board of Radiology (ABR) — Radiation Oncology initial certification pathway
medical.boardStatus: ABR is the specialty certifying board for the physician Radiation Oncology pathway. The official pathway includes an initial Qualifying Exam with Medical Physics, Radiation and Cancer Biology, and Clinical Radiation Oncology components, followed by an Oral Certifying Exam. It is not a separate board examination for each modality. Johns Hopkins official residency directory labels this specific programme “ACGME Accredited”; ACGME is the programme accreditor, not the certifying board. Checked 2026-10-07.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABR eligibility requires prescribed clinical year, accredited four-year radiation oncology residency or an official alternate pathway, examinations, valid medical licensure and ethical standing; the board sets applicable completion and eligibility windows. This independent study course provides no accredited training, case logs, eligibility, licensure, procedure competence or certification and cannot guarantee any exam result. Verify current details directly with ABR before making decisions.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Radiation Oncology Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official department page describes a four-year clinical physician residency, at least 36 months required clinical rotations per page, a potential 12-month elective/specialty/research allocation, weekly academic sessions and weekly physics/radiobiology courses. These are institutional summaries, not a complete public lecture syllabus or evidence of equal didactic hours. Separate official residency directory calls the program ACGME Accredited; see programmeSourceScope.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Only the institutional variant in the supplied MED-118 packet is included: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Radiation Oncology Residency. The exact official residency listing reports four years and ACGME Accredited. The department page describes a clinical physician residency, 36 months required clinical rotations and optional elective/specialty/research time up to 12 months; no separate combined physician residency, disease-site track, or co-board programme was established by the cited programme pages. Research year/electives are not a research-only/non-physician degree. This is not a generic radiation oncology directory category. No Harvard variant was in this packet and none is silently added.
sourceCaveats: ABR study-guide domain weights are explicitly historical guidance for periods named in those guides; the linked clinical guide lists ranges generally in effect for 2025 and does not predict item counts.
ACGME describes accredited graduate medical education; an independent asynchronous course has no patient-care supervision, assessments/clinical Milestones, case logs, accreditation or admissions.
Institution programme information is a public summary and not the full local syllabus. Inaccessibility of proprietary or login-only material was not bypassed; none is counted.

Rad Onc Talks videos were selected from one public channel feed; the video list reported 101 entries. The administrative “Billing 101” item was excluded. The remaining 100 entries each had a positive exact duration field. Canonical IDs are unique. Public listing/playback does not give rehost or embed permission.

No commercial reuse of any protected video or patient images is inferred. Only original link-out is used. Radiopaedia re-use conditions are especially restrictive for commercial material; school commercial status was not assumed.
No clinical guideline recommendation or patient-specific treatment is provided. Verify contemporary disease-specific guidelines, regulations, board policy and local protocols when relevant.
The training program may involve a research year or elective but remains a clinical physician residency with supervised experience, distinct from a research-only/non-physician supplement.

topicGaps: No public complete Hopkins lecture schedule or comprehensive institution-owned lecture series was found; its page describes recurring didactics but does not expose a full curriculum or itemized hours.

Recorded lecture coverage is strong for core adult CNS, head/neck, thoracic, breast, GI, GU, gynecologic and hematologic/pediatric topics. Depth and currency vary by video; board study guides are dated (clinical outline labeled 2025, physics guide 2023, biology guide 2022).

Selected topics needing focused source review/optional new teaching include detailed brachytherapy workflow, systemic radionuclide safety, particle therapy uncertainties, image guidance/QA, trial-applicability critique, rare/benign disease, pediatric late effects and site-specific contemporary guidance. Planned clips below are not ready videos and add zero counted hours.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner groups external-beam radiotherapy, brachytherapy and a swallowed radiopharmaceutical together as “the same local technique.” Which distinction is best supported by the NCI overview?

options.text: External beam is directed from outside; brachytherapy places a solid source in/near a site; systemic radiopharmaceutical therapy travels through the body.
All three require the radiation source to remain outside the patient.
Brachytherapy and systemic radiopharmaceuticals are identical because both are internal.
External beam is necessarily systemic while a swallowed agent is necessarily local.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI distinguishes external beam as an external local treatment, solid-source brachytherapy as internal local treatment, and liquid systemic radiation as systemic.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hypothetical physics exercise compares 30 Gy in five equal 6-Gy fractions with α/β=3 Gy using BED=nd[1+d/(α/β)]. What value follows from the stated model?

options.text: 48 Gy3
60 Gy3
90 Gy3

practiceQuestions.rationale: BED=5×6×(1+6/3)=30×3=90 Gy3. This is a model calculation only; it does not determine a clinical dose or compare actual plans without clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a board-style consultation outline, what evidence should be established before a treatment option is discussed as if applicable?

options.text: Tissue diagnosis and site-specific staging context, relevant patient factors/goals, and multidisciplinary options.
A radiation technique selected from a video title.
Only an imaging impression; pathology and staging are irrelevant.
A single dose value without intent, field, toxicity, or evidence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR clinical outline includes epidemiology/pathology, anatomy, diagnosis/staging, treatment selection, patient-context and follow-up; a learning exercise should surface missing evidence and options rather than assume applicability.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the ABR physician radiation oncology initial certification pathway is correct on the official ABR page checked 2026-10-07?

options.text: It is a single online course certificate that replaces residency.
The Qualifying Exam has physics, radiation/cancer biology and clinical components, followed by an Oral Certifying Exam; clinical training/licensure eligibility requirements also apply.
The physics exam alone certifies a physician.
Passing an independent video quiz creates board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR describes a four-year accredited RO residency after one clinical year, a three-part Qualifying Exam plus Oral Certifying Exam, licensure and ethics criteria. An independent course cannot confer eligibility or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational plan-review exercise asks what the ABR physics guide explicitly includes. Which set is accurate?

options.text: Basic physics, measurement, treatment planning, imaging, brachytherapy, advanced procedures and safety/QA.
Only histopathology and systemic chemotherapy.
Only dose units, with no planning or safety.
Only the physician oral examination categories.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR physics study guide lists seven domains including planning, imaging, brachytherapy, special procedures and safety/QA.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which interpretation of an institutional rotation description is most careful?

options.text: A public training page describes real supervised GME experiences; it does not license an outside learner or establish public lecture-hours for the institution.
A clinical rotation description means the same patient care can be performed by anyone who reads about it.
A year of research is equivalent to a year of supervised clinical practice.
A programme website proves every resident receives identical procedural competency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins describes required clinical rotations and research options; ACGME requirements require supervised educational and clinical experience. These cannot be replicated by an online curriculum.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public teaching image is visible on a case site. What must a course author do before incorporating the image into a paid or publicly hosted video?

options.text: Assume free-to-view means unrestricted copying.
Rehost it with identifying clinical details cropped.
Review source-specific license, attribution and commercial terms; link only until permission is verified.
Treat a hyperlink as automatic reproduction permission.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia specifies CC BY-NC-SA conditions and warns that paid/monetized uses can require permission; a link does not grant rehosting rights. Never use identifiable patient records.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner encounters possible new neurologic symptoms in a linked educational scenario. What is the safe educational response?

options.text: Use the public clip to independently prescribe an emergency treatment.
Flag that this may be urgent, communicate and escalate to qualified clinicians/local protocols; do not manage the real patient from a course.
Wait for a planned clip.
Infer diagnosis from a single image and ignore clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ARRO ROCK resource is an educational emergency framework, while the course does not authorize real patient management. Escalation is a safety principle, not a treatment order.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the best interpretation of the 2026 ACGME radiation oncology requirements for this independent online curriculum?

options.text: A 48-month independent e-learning course is an accredited residency.
ACGME sets GME standards that include 48 months of RO education and at least 36 clinical months; online learning cannot provide the supervised clinical experiences or accreditation.
450 public videos replace simulation and case supervision.
A self-study learner becomes board eligible after completing all unit objectives.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The effective 2026 ACGME requirements specify a 48-month educational program with at least 36 clinical months; they require supervised experiences beyond passive video study.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner uses the ABR clinical outline to organize a study plan. What is the valid use of published category percentages?

options.text: They are exact prediction of the next candidate’s exam.
They are historical guidance labeled by ABR and can support coverage planning, not guarantee question counts, readiness or passing.
They replace current guidelines and trial evidence.
They authorize practice in each category.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR page expressly notes weight ranges were generally in effect for the 2025 exam and are guidance rather than precise scorable-item counts.

Basic anatomy, pathology, imaging, clinical oncology, pharmacology, biostatistics and consent/privacy vocabulary.

objectives: Map radiation oncology decision-making to the published ABR Radiation Oncology clinical domains without claiming a pass standard.

assignment.title: Evidence-based multidisciplinary case conference brief
assignment.instructions: Write a 1,200–1,800 word analysis of one explicitly fictional cancer vignette. State what is known and missing; describe pathology/staging and evidence questions; compare plausible modality roles without prescribing; discuss patient goals, normal-tissue concerns, safety, evidence applicability, and follow-up. Use at least four current authoritative references including one ABR domain reference and one openly accessible clinical evidence source. If using eContour, link to the case and do not reproduce its images or records.
assignment.passRule: For self-study feedback only; no board-equivalent or clinical competence interpretation.

assessment.formative: Ten original questions with rationales, unit exercises, and short reflection after each linked recording.
assessment.summative: Evidence-based case-conference brief plus a structured 10-minute oral synthesis using a fictional case.
assessment.criteria: Use the assignment rubric; require corrections of unsupported claims, missing uncertainty, privacy lapse, or any representation of self-study as authorization.
assessment.limitations: Unvalidated self-study assessment; not official ABR questions, not a predictor of board passing and not clinical competency assessment.

topicGaps: Media floor: satisfied by 104.766944 verified unique accessible free recordings (36 h target exceeded); this is viewing availability only, not rendered original content, residency credit, clinical competence, board readiness or authorization.

Institution-specific coverage remains unavailable: public Harvard/DFCI and Johns Hopkins programme pages do not disclose complete lecture libraries, resident attendance requirements or institutional case volumes. The public recordings are independent education, not those institutions’ curricula.

The accessible lecture catalog now covers core physics/biology, plan evaluation, major adult sites, palliative presentations, trial appraisal, pediatric CNS and sarcoma, and multiple hematologic sites. Remaining sparse/unverified areas include benign indications, eye/orbit and rare skin entities, leukemia/myeloma, uncommon GU and gynecologic primaries, and detailed QA/source-emergency protocol; use current authoritative readings and local supervised instruction.

The Rad Onc Talks channel includes recent content but spans topics and publication dates; the Zurich grand rounds are case/trial discussions. Neither collection is a vetted current treatment guideline. Re-check any treatment claim against current primary guidance and disclose historical trial context.

ASTRO ARRO publicly lists additional useful series; some items lead to embed-only or login/member registration resources and were not counted without observed accessible duration. No paid ASTRO Academy study guide, eContour images, or registration-gated playback was used.
No free public complete Harvard/DFCI or Johns Hopkins residency/fellowship lecture library was verified. Institutional programme descriptions are not lecture recordings or transferable credit.

The ABR 2026-posted clinical guide states its broad domain ranges generally apply to the 2025 exam and are guidance, not exact item percentages. Confirm current ABR requirements, staging and toxicity conventions before future use.

No human clinician review has been performed. The recordings and original scripts require expert review before any clinical reliance; this course is not clinical advice, an accredited programme, or a substitute for supervised training.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This single adult physician radiation-oncology curriculum deduplicates the common ABR specialty while preserving each exact public institutional programme variant. It includes two separately named DFCI clinical fellowships, the separate HROP and Johns Hopkins residencies, and Hopkins Proton Therapy ASTP. The Hopkins NSTP label is retained as a generic individualized directory category, not represented as a fixed curriculum. Medical-physics residency/fellowship, medical-student elective and research activity are explicitly supplements/exclusions, not physician board tracks. The published ABR clinical guide includes pediatric and benign indications inside the RO examination domains; no independent pediatric RO board/programme was inferred. No institutional lecture series was assumed to be public or transferable.
sourceCaveats: Public institutional pages describe programme structure and selected rotations/didactics but do not expose full institutional lecture catalogues or guarantee current individual eligibility.

topicGaps: Media floor: satisfied by 104.766944 verified unique accessible free recordings (36 h target exceeded); this is viewing availability only, not rendered original content, residency credit, clinical competence, board readiness or authorization.

Institution-specific coverage remains unavailable: public Harvard/DFCI and Johns Hopkins programme pages do not disclose complete lecture libraries, resident attendance requirements or institutional case volumes. The public recordings are independent education, not those institutions’ curricula.

The accessible lecture catalog now covers core physics/biology, plan evaluation, major adult sites, palliative presentations, trial appraisal, pediatric CNS and sarcoma, and multiple hematologic sites. Remaining sparse/unverified areas include benign indications, eye/orbit and rare skin entities, leukemia/myeloma, uncommon GU and gynecologic primaries, and detailed QA/source-emergency protocol; use current authoritative readings and local supervised instruction.

The Rad Onc Talks channel includes recent content but spans topics and publication dates; the Zurich grand rounds are case/trial discussions. Neither collection is a vetted current treatment guideline. Re-check any treatment claim against current primary guidance and disclose historical trial context.

ASTRO ARRO publicly lists additional useful series; some items lead to embed-only or login/member registration resources and were not counted without observed accessible duration. No paid ASTRO Academy study guide, eContour images, or registration-gated playback was used.
No free public complete Harvard/DFCI or Johns Hopkins residency/fellowship lecture library was verified. Institutional programme descriptions are not lecture recordings or transferable credit.

The ABR 2026-posted clinical guide states its broad domain ranges generally apply to the 2025 exam and are guidance, not exact item percentages. Confirm current ABR requirements, staging and toxicity conventions before future use.

No human clinician review has been performed. The recordings and original scripts require expert review before any clinical reliance; this course is not clinical advice, an accredited programme, or a substitute for supervised training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient is referred for possible radiotherapy, but the referral packet lacks final histology and complete staging. What is the strongest next educational reasoning step?

options.text: Select a standard dose based on the suspected primary site.
Identify the missing diagnostic/staging inputs and coordinate review before asserting a modality plan.
Assume the referral diagnosis is final and proceed to treatment.
Use a public video case as a substitute for the patient workup.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR clinical guide includes diagnosis, staging, modality selection, and treatment planning; a referral label is not a substitute for confirmed diagnostic context. The exercise concerns process, not clinical advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a simplified linear-quadratic BED calculation, which statement is correct?

options.text: BED = nd × (1 + d/(α/β)); its clinical use depends on model assumptions and tissue-specific inputs.
BED = n + d and is independent of α/β.
Equal BED proves two schedules are clinically interchangeable.
BED applies only to protons.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The conventional model relation is BED = nd[1+d/(α/β)]. It is a model and does not prove clinical equivalence; assumptions and context matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which term denotes the need for oxygen to enhance radiation-mediated fixation of damage in many experimental settings?

options.text: Inverse-square law
Oxygen effect
Radioactive equilibrium
Range straggling

practiceQuestions.rationale: The oxygen effect is a foundational radiation biology concept listed in ABR’s radiation/cancer biology exam content.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is reviewing a plan image and sees target coverage and an organ-at-risk DVH. What is the appropriate educational conclusion?

options.text: The plan is approved because the target curve looks acceptable.
Interpret the metrics within prescription, contour, constraint, and QA context; a learner cannot independently approve treatment.
The DVH alone confirms setup reproducibility.
Ignore image guidance if a DVH exists.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR includes target/OAR dose, DVH, constraints, precision, and QA; no single graph establishes safe delivery, and this course does not confer clinical privileges.

practiceQuestions.stem: An anonymized educational contouring resource requires free registration to open cases. What is the best rights practice?

options.text: Download and rehost the case because access is free.
Use the case through the linked site under its terms; do not copy or redistribute images.
Treat absence of patient identifiers as an open license.
Replace institutional access controls with a shared login.

practiceQuestions.rationale: eContour has free case viewing but papers report registration is needed; free-to-view does not grant reuse rights. Link only and follow current terms.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly characterizes the board pathway for radiation oncology in the United States?

options.text: Every clinical fellowship has a separate ABR board examination.
The ABR Radiation Oncology pathway includes a qualifying exam with physics, biology, and clinical components and an oral certifying exam; fellowship name does not itself confer certification.
A Harvard or Hopkins course automatically grants ABR eligibility.
A proton therapy fellowship is a separate ABR primary specialty certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR describes initial RO certification with three qualifying parts and oral certifying exam; eligibility requires qualifying prior clinical training and accredited residency/pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about board recognition of the named proton, CNS radiosurgery/radiotherapy, and brachytherapy training tracks is supported?

options.text: Each is a separately named ABR subspecialty certificate.
They are institutional clinical fellowship tracks; ABR separately lists pain medicine as an RO-accessible subspecialty, not these tracks.
They each confer independent state licenses.
They establish competency after watching course videos.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABR subspecialty page lists pain medicine under radiation oncology; institutional named fellowships do not by themselves imply separate ABR certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: For an older public lecture discussing clinical treatment, the learner should:

options.text: Adopt all treatment claims because the presenter is a physician.
Use it for stable concepts only and verify current clinical recommendations against current authoritative sources.
Assume the video’s upload age has no effect on clinical validity.
Count a lecture as current guideline evidence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public lectures are teaching resources, not current clinical guidelines; the playlist is an older series. Use current board/guideline sources for clinical claims.

practiceQuestions.stem: During a simulated treatment-workflow exercise, image registration appears inconsistent with expected anatomy. What is the best safety response?

options.text: Proceed because treatment time is limited.
Pause/escalate for verification under the local safety workflow; do not independently alter patient care.
Manually copy a correction from a web image.
Silently omit the discrepancy from the record.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABR requirements include precision/errors, QA, patient/personnel safety, and error communication. In live care, follow local chain-of-command and protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner compares two randomized-trial regimens and wants to apply results to an older patient with different comorbidities. Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Treat the trial result as a universal rule.
Check population, intervention, outcomes, harms, uncertainty, applicability, and patient goals with a clinical team.
Ignore the comparator and use the abstract conclusion alone.
Claim a guaranteed outcome from a relative effect.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Evidence must be appraised for design, outcomes, external validity, toxicity, and patient priorities; NCI PDQ is an evidence-informed resource for professional decision-making, not a patient-specific order.

unitMap.text: Thoracic oncology scope, risk, screening and prevention
Diagnostic pathway, histology and tissue stewardship
Anatomic staging and multidisciplinary formulation
Molecular pathology, predictive biomarkers and resistance
Early-stage and resectable NSCLC
Locally advanced NSCLC and multimodality care
Metastatic NSCLC: first-line selection and response assessment
Relapsed disease, CNS metastases and resistance
Small-cell lung cancer and high-grade neuroendocrine disease
Mesothelioma, thymic tumors and rare thoracic malignancies
Treatment toxicities, supportive care, survivorship and communication
Clinical trials, research methods, ethics and evidence updating

topicGaps: The target is 36 verified recording hours; 11.884167 unique accessible free recording hours are supported by observed runtimes, leaving 24.115833 verified hours unfilled.

Most new recordings emphasize diagnosis, tissue workflow, biomarkers, perioperative NSCLC, staging, and selected treatment complications. There is no verified full-length clinician lecture coverage sufficient for metastatic NSCLC treatment/progression reasoning, dedicated SCLC, mesothelioma/thymic and other rare thoracic malignancies, trial methods/ethics, or supportive care/toxicity; these domains retain source-reading and original teaching needs.

The 2021–2022 recordings are historical. Biomarker standards, staging editions, trial results, treatment indications, and safety statements need point-of-use checking against current primary guidance and FDA labeling; historical recordings do not close current-practice gaps.

IASLC’s official catalogue lists free 60-minute on-demand webinars on limited-stage SCLC and mesothelioma pathology, but a directly accessible full player without sign-in was not confirmed; these listings are not included in verified hours.
Hands-on pathology, imaging, staging procedures, biopsy/procedural competence, prescribing, infusion, toxicity management, and real patient communication cannot be earned through this course.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardStatus.specialtyExam: No separate thoracic oncology certification board or thoracic oncology board examination identified in ABIM’s published certification roster/policy as checked 2026-10-07. The specialty name denotes an institutional clinical/research fellowship focus, not a distinct board-certified subspecialty.
boardStatus.relatedExams: ABIM offers Medical Oncology certification and separately Hematology certification. Board examination eligibility is governed by ABIM policy and depends on prior internal medicine certification, qualifying accredited training, licensure and competency requirements; the Dana-Farber advanced fellowship alone is not a substitute for that training.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent course completion confers no ABIM eligibility. Dana-Farber’s public page states that applicants must have completed medical oncology training (minimum two years) or hematology/oncology (minimum three years), and must be eligible for a limited or permanent Massachusetts medical license; it also gives licensing-examination qualifications and other conditions. These are institutional applicant requirements, not a guarantee of appointment, medical license, ABIM eligibility, or certification. ABIM’s published policy requires qualifying accredited U.S./Canadian subspecialty fellowship training for certification. Confirm current terms with Dana-Farber, the relevant licensing authority and ABIM.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Official institutional offering verified directly from its public Dana-Farber page. Packet title abbreviated as “Thoracic Oncology Advanced Fellowship”; preserve the exact official title and institutional variant above. It is a clinical/investigative physician advanced fellowship, not an ACGME-accredited residency, stand-alone board specialty, generic directory category, combined board program, PA/pharmacy track, or research-only postdoctoral appointment. The public description says ~80% research and ~20% clinical and lists one weekly clinic day plus weekly tumor board. This independent course does not reproduce the private institutional curriculum. No Harvard/Johns Hopkins second variant was established for this item.
sourceCaveats: The institutional page is the source for this specific fellowship; ABIM and ACGME documents describe board/training pathways and do not accredit or certify this Dana-Farber advanced fellowship.

unknownDurationItems.title: Moving from Palliation to Cure: Progress in the Treatment of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (Yale Cancer Center Grand Rounds; public video candidate)
unknownDurationItems.reason: Accessible duration not structurally supported by evidence.

topicGaps: The target is 36 verified recording hours; 11.884167 unique accessible free recording hours are supported by observed runtimes, leaving 24.115833 verified hours unfilled.

Most new recordings emphasize diagnosis, tissue workflow, biomarkers, perioperative NSCLC, staging, and selected treatment complications. There is no verified full-length clinician lecture coverage sufficient for metastatic NSCLC treatment/progression reasoning, dedicated SCLC, mesothelioma/thymic and other rare thoracic malignancies, trial methods/ethics, or supportive care/toxicity; these domains retain source-reading and original teaching needs.

The 2021–2022 recordings are historical. Biomarker standards, staging editions, trial results, treatment indications, and safety statements need point-of-use checking against current primary guidance and FDA labeling; historical recordings do not close current-practice gaps.

IASLC’s official catalogue lists free 60-minute on-demand webinars on limited-stage SCLC and mesothelioma pathology, but a directly accessible full player without sign-in was not confirmed; these listings are not included in verified hours.
Hands-on pathology, imaging, staging procedures, biopsy/procedural competence, prescribing, infusion, toxicity management, and real patient communication cannot be earned through this course.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with newly diagnosed metastatic lung adenocarcinoma has tissue adequate for additional testing. Which approach best supports an initial systemic-treatment discussion?

options.text: Choose a regimen from smoking history alone.
Review histology, stage, comprehensive relevant biomarker results and PD-L1 status, patient factors, and current dated guidance before discussing options.
Start immunotherapy before reviewing actionable-driver results because PD-L1 is always dominant.
Defer any molecular testing until progression.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Treatment decisions are stage- and biomarker-sensitive; NCI PDQ organizes NSCLC options by stage and includes targeted and immune-based choices. Current FDA labels change, so verify date and indication. Smoking history alone does not establish biomarker status.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional metastatic adenocarcinoma report identifies an established actionable EGFR alteration. What is the soundest reasoning principle?

options.text: Use the driver result to inform treatment options and verify the current setting-specific evidence and label.
Ignore the result if the person has ever smoked.
Assume all EGFR alterations have the same sensitivity and resistance profile.
Treat the biomarker report as a substitute for staging.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Molecularly targeted therapy is tied to particular alterations and indications; verify variant-level significance and current stage-specific guidance. Biomarkers do not replace staging.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees a single CT report describing a lung mass and mediastinal nodes. Which statement about stage is most appropriate?

options.text: The CT report alone definitively supplies clinical and pathologic stage.
Stage should be assigned only after checking all relevant anatomic and distant-disease data, applicable staging edition, and any needed nodal/pathology information.
Use the ninth edition only for mesothelioma, not lung cancer.
TNM staging does not influence treatment intent.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IASLC provides current ninth-edition staging cards for thoracic malignancies; staging requires complete case facts and clinical versus pathologic stage distinction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A screening program participant receives a positive low-dose CT result. What is the correct conceptual next step?

options.text: Call the result lung cancer and initiate treatment.
Explain screening is not diagnosis and arrange evaluation under the applicable diagnostic follow-up pathway.
Repeat annual screening indefinitely without evaluating the finding.
Assume every positive screen is a false positive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening tests have false-positive and other harms; a positive screen requires diagnostic assessment and shared decision-making, not a cancer diagnosis by itself.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional small-cell lung cancer case is being formulated. Which staging framework should anchor initial treatment discussion in the NCI PDQ?

options.text: Limited-stage versus extensive-stage, while retaining appropriate anatomic staging and multidisciplinary context.
NSCLC driver-positive versus driver-negative only.
Localized versus distant SEER summary stage only.
Never stage SCLC because it is systemic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCI SCLC PDQ organizes therapy by limited-stage, extensive-stage, and recurrent disease. Avoid transplanting the NSCLC branch structure.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pleural tumor has an epithelioid morphology that could be confused with adenocarcinoma. What is a defensible learning response?

options.text: Declare mesothelioma based on location alone.
Request expert pathology correlation and appropriate immunohistochemical workup; recognize the differential and stage separately.
Classify it as NSCLC because all pleural carcinomas are lung primaries.
Use a patient-facing brochure as a histopathology reference.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ notes diagnostic overlap of epithelioid mesothelioma and adenocarcinoma and describes the role of tissue and immunohistochemistry. This is a pathology-team task, not a self-study diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: An oncology team considers enrolling a person in a lung-cancer clinical trial. Which action best reflects research ethics and informed consent?

options.text: Treat the registry listing as proof of eligibility and guaranteed benefit.
Review protocol-specific eligibility, risks, alternatives, voluntariness and consent with the study team; confirm current availability.
Enroll without explaining randomization if the trial is standard at the institution.
Use a research study to bypass standard review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI describes trial processes, participant responsibilities, informed consent and oversight; trial listings are not guarantees of eligibility, access or benefit.

practiceQuestions.stem: A lecture recorded several years ago describes a lung-cancer drug as investigational. What should a learner do before applying the statement to current practice?

options.text: Assume the lecture remains current because it is from a recognized institution.
Check the current FDA label and updated authoritative guidance, identify the indication and approval status date, and note uncertainty.
Infer approval from a conference abstract.
Use a social media summary instead of the label.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA warns it does not announce every oncology approval or label update and directs users to Drugs@FDA for latest product information. Date-check is essential in a fast-moving field.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner wants to use CT images from the TCIA NSCLC-Radiomics collection in an educational slide. What is the appropriate first step?

options.text: Download and republish any image because public access means public domain.
Review the collection license and data-use policy, cite the dataset, preserve de-identification, and use only as permitted; otherwise link rather than rehost.
Copy patient-level clinical CSV details into an open course.
Use the data for commercial purposes under CC BY-NC without further review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA describes its de-identification process and lists NSCLC-Radiomics image/clinical data under CC BY-NC 3.0 with required citation and usage policy. Noncommercial terms do not permit unrestricted commercial re-use; public download does not erase attribution or privacy duties.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient asks whether an outcome statistic predicts exactly what will happen to them. What is the best response?

options.text: Yes; population survival statistics give a precise individual forecast.
Explain that population estimates support context, not an exact individual prediction, and discuss individual factors and goals with the treating team.
Avoid any discussion of uncertainty.
Provide a guaranteed result if the patient chooses treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SEER explicitly notes population survival statistics cannot predict an individual course because people and responses differ. Communication should preserve uncertainty and avoid guarantees.
